questiontext.text: Which best describes the core mechanism of Fibonacci search?

answer.text: Narrow the sorted range using split points derived from Fibonacci numbers instead of always halving

feedback.text: Correct — successive Fibonacci numbers determine the probe positions.

answer.text: Scan every element in order from the start

feedback.text: That is linear search.

answer.text: Always compare the exact middle element to halve the interval

feedback.text: That is binary search; Fibonacci search splits by Fibonacci numbers, not exactly in half.

answer.text: Estimate the probe position from the target's value

feedback.text: That is interpolation search.

generalfeedback.text: Fibonacci search uses consecutive Fibonacci numbers to choose split points, examining elements toward the front of the range.

questiontext.text: How many comparisons (time complexity) does Fibonacci search need in the worst case over n elements?

feedback.text: Correct — like binary search, it shrinks the range logarithmically.
That is linear search; Fibonacci search is logarithmic.
That is interpolation search's average on uniform data.
Too large; Fibonacci search is O(log n).

generalfeedback.text: Fibonacci search shrinks the interval by a constant factor each step, giving O(log n) comparisons.

questiontext.text: What precondition must the input satisfy for Fibonacci search to work correctly?

feedback.text: Correct — like binary search, it relies on order to discard part of the range.
No — order is required.

answer.text: The values must be uniformly distributed

feedback.text: That matters for interpolation search, not Fibonacci search.

answer.text: The array length must itself be a Fibonacci number

feedback.text: No — the algorithm just uses the smallest Fibonacci number ≥ n; the length need not be Fibonacci.

generalfeedback.text: Fibonacci search requires a sorted array; it then uses Fibonacci numbers only to pick split points.

questiontext.text: What is a distinctive advantage of Fibonacci search over binary search?

answer.text: It computes split points using only addition and subtraction, avoiding division

feedback.text: Correct — historically useful when division or mid-index computation was costly.
No — it still requires a sorted array.
No — it is O(log n), like binary search.

answer.text: It needs no comparisons at all

feedback.text: No — it still compares elements to the target.

generalfeedback.text: Fibonacci search advances its indices with additions/subtractions of Fibonacci numbers, so it needs no division to find a midpoint.

questiontext.text: Which statements about Fibonacci search are true? (select all that apply)

feedback.text: Yes — order is needed to discard part of the range.

answer.text: It uses only addition and subtraction, with no division, to find split points

feedback.text: Yes — that is its historical selling point.

answer.text: It runs in O(n log n) time

feedback.text: No — it makes O(log n) comparisons.
No — it requires sorted input.

generalfeedback.text: Fibonacci search: O(log n) comparisons, sorted input, division-free split points via Fibonacci numbers, O(1) space.

questiontext.text: Fibonacci search requires the input array to be sorted.

feedback.text: Correct — it relies on order to eliminate part of the range.
No — like binary search, it needs sorted input.

questiontext.text: Fibonacci search must perform a division to compute each split point.

feedback.text: No — it advances indices using additions and subtractions of Fibonacci numbers, avoiding division.
Correct — it needs only addition and subtraction, no division.

questiontext.text: The split points of this search are chosen using numbers from the ______ sequence. Name it (one word).

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
